name: Sustainable HRM – definition
purpose: What makes an HRM strategy “sustainable”? Four elements of the definition.

parts.label: Inside & outside
points: Impact inside and outside the organization

parts.label: Side effects
points: Controlling for unintended side effects and negative feedback

apply: Test a proposed HR practice against all four elements
Name the unintended side effect explicitly (e.g. cost cut → workload → burnout → turnover)
pitfalls: Equating sustainable HRM with “green HRM” only – the social and financial goals count too
example: “Adoption of HRM strategies and practices that enable the achievement of financial, social and ecological goals, with an impact inside and outside of the organization and over a long-term time horizon while controlling for unintended side effects and negative feedback.”

name: Triple Bottom Line
purpose: Which three dimensions does corporate sustainability – and sustainable HRM – have to balance?
apply: Score each HR option on the three dimensions (+ / 0 / −)
Identify the trade-off: which dimension pays for the gain in another?
Recommend the options that balance the three, or that mitigate the losing dimension
pitfalls: Only listing benefits – the exercise is about trade-offs (e.g. AI recruitment: cheaper but biased)
example: HR Director exercise (fast fashion): freezing recruitment saves money (financial +) but raises workloads (social −); a living wage in the supply chain is social + but costly; reskilling (€5m) is costly short term but social + and financial + long term.

name: Strategic HRM vs sustainable HRM philosophy
origin: Kramar (2014); Macke & Genari (2019); Ren & Jackson (2020); Stahl et al. (2020)
purpose: Is sustainable HRM a new approach to people management? Seven contrasts.

parts.label: Strategic HRM philosophy
points: Financial performance is the most important goal

parts.label: Sustainable HRM philosophy
points: Beyond own boundaries: communities and other organizations
Environmental, social and financial performance of equal importance

apply: Place the case firm's HR function on each of the seven contrasts
Argue which shift would matter most for the case problem
pitfalls: Presenting sustainable HRM as anti-business – financial performance still counts, just not alone

name: Reasons for sustainable HRM
purpose: Why do companies implement sustainable HRM practices (and refrain from unsustainable ones)?
apply: Identify the firm's motive – it predicts how far the practice will go
Compliance = minimum; instrumental and mission-led go beyond regulations and laws
pitfalls: Assuming one motive – firms often mix them (e.g. EU pay-transparency compliance + employer branding)

name: Sustainable HRM practices by dimension
purpose: Which concrete HR practices serve each dimension of the triple bottom line?

parts.label: Financial
points: Leadership development: long-term investment in employees

parts.label: Ecological
points: Hire employees who embrace sustainability goals

parts.label: Social
points: Positive social and physical work environment
Invest in physical and psychological health
Eliminate child and forced labour in the supply chain

apply: Pick practices from each column to build a balanced recommendation
Show the trade-off each one creates (brainstorm task: 3 HR practices with a sustainability trade-off)
pitfalls: Listing practices without linking them to the case problem

name: Sins of commission and omission
purpose: How can HR harm people – by what it does and by what it fails to do?

parts.label: Commission – HR contributes to a problem
points: Layoffs purely to raise short-term profitability

parts.label: Omission – HR fails to prevent a problem
points: Failing to develop workers whose jobs are threatened by AI

apply: Scan the case for both: what HR actively does wrong, and what it tolerates
Recommend a fix for each sin – omission is often the easier one to miss
pitfalls: Only criticizing active decisions – silence and inaction count as well
